description: COSMOS & VISION is a multidisciplinary team developing an innovative approach to astronaut health monitoring during space missions. By integrating biological, psychological and social data, our project aims to transform complex health information into meaningful insights to support personalised monitoring and decision-making. Our goal is to turn data into understanding, both in space and potentially on Earth.
summary:
COSMOS & VISION is an onboard health system that lets a crew without a doctor detect, understand and act on medical problems during long missions, when Earth can be up to 40 minutes away.
COSMOS (Comprehensive Onboard Space-health Monitoring and Operational Support) is the hardware: a smart shirt (ECG, breathing, lung ventilation, muscle, body composition), a wristband (pulse, SpO₂, blood pressure, stress), cabin air sensors, and an opt-in camera and microphone. 
VISION (Visual Integrated System for Interactive Onboard Navigation of vitals) is the onboard app. It compares every reading with the astronaut's own baseline adjusted to microgravity, applies NASA-STD-3001 and NEWS2 limits, and forecasts when a vital sign is heading towards critical. The crew sees one clear traffic light per module (Biological, Psychological, Social, Ship) and an anatomical 3D digital twin built on the NIH HuBMAP Human Reference Atlas. Every alert links to its scientific evidence, a step-by-step protocol, the exact medical-kit location and just-in-time training. Our models were trained and validated on open PhysioNet data and give far fewer false alarms than fixed thresholds. 
Everything runs on board, without Earth. This matters because on a Mars mission the crew must be its own clinic: VISION turns raw signals into clear, explainable decisions, and the same approach can help isolated people on Earth.
details:
COSMOS and VISION is an onboard health system for long-duration missions, where Earth can be up to 40 minutes away and the crew may have no doctor on board.

COSMOS (Comprehensive Onboard Space-health Monitoring and Operational Support)(hardware concept) collects the data:

- Smart shirt: ECG, heart rate and HRV, breathing, lung ventilation (EIT), muscle (EMG/EIM), body composition (BIA), skin temperature and movement.

- Wristband: pulse and SpO₂ (PPG), blood pressure (micro cuff), stress (EDA). Its NFC tag identifies the astronaut and unlocks VISION with their own data.

- Cabin sensors: CO₂, O₂, pressure, temperature and humidity.

- Opt-in camera and microphone: posture and voice features, processed on board.

VISION (Visual Integrated System for Interactive Onboard Navigation of vitals) (the onboard app) works in three steps:

1. Detect: every reading is compared with the astronaut's own baseline, adjusted to microgravity. Clinical rules (NEWS2) decide what is critical, a personal model raises early alerts, and a forecast model warns when a vital sign is heading to critical.

2. Assess: risks are linked to NASA Human Research Program evidence, NASA-STD-3001 limits and peer-reviewed studies.

3. Respond: one traffic light per module and one clear action. Step-by-step protocols, the exact medical-kit location, just-in-time training, and a record that is sent to Earth in each communication window.

The interface has 8 modules: Biological (an anatomical 3D digital twin built from the NIH HuBMAP Human Reference Atlas), Psychological (a daily check-in based on the NASA Alertness and Mood Survey, plus a voice check), Social (a weekly crew check-in), CDSS (clinical decision support), JITT (just-in-time training), Medical Inventory, Ship (cabin air on a floor plan of the ISS) and Medical Record.

BENEFITS

- Personal, not population thresholds: with the same data, VISION gave about 12 times fewer false alarms than fixed rules (2.2 vs 26.2 alerts per day, on 20 people, leave-one-subject-out) and detected 94% of injected tachycardia episodes.

- Microgravity-aware: normal adaptation to space (about +1 °C body temperature, lower blood pressure) is not flagged as illness.

- Explainable: every alert shows why, the source it comes from and what to do. There is no language model, so it cannot invent medical information.

- Fully autonomous: it runs on the onboard computer without a link to Earth.

INTENDED IMPACT

VISION lets a crew act as its own clinic on the way to Mars: problems are seen early, and a non-physician can follow a clear protocol under stress. The same approach can serve polar stations, ships, remote clinics and people living alone far from a doctor.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGIES

- Front end: React, TypeScript, Vite and Tailwind CSS, deployed on Vercel.

- 3D anatomy: Three.js with glTF organs from the HuBMAP Human Reference Atlas (NIH 3D, CC BY 4.0), compressed with glTF-Transform.

- Charts: Recharts.

- Machine learning: Python. The personal anomaly model was trained on PhysioNet MMASH and nsr2db and validated with chf2db. The forecast neural network was trained on 6,000 ICU patients from PhysioNet 2019 and reached AUROC 0.67 vs 0.62 for NEWS2 alone.

- Live sensing in the browser: MediaPipe Pose (posture), Web Audio API (voice features inspired by eGeMAPS/openSMILE) and Web NFC (wristband login).

- AI assistants: Claude for coding, research and writing; ChatGPT for images and icons. The team reviewed and directed all outputs.

- Hardware: the shirt and wristband are designed concepts; in the demo their signals are simulated from published scenarios.

CREATIVITY

- A 3D digital twin that joins a real anatomical atlas with each astronaut's live data: tap an organ to see its variables, trend, risk, protocols and evidence.

- One closed loop from early warning to action: the risk warned earlier becomes the starting point of the emergency protocol, which links to the kit slot and the training lesson.

- Body, mind, crew and the ship's air in one icon-first interface, designed for someone who feels unwell and cannot read paragraphs.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Safety: rules decide emergencies; AI only adds early warnings. The final decision always belongs to the crew medical officer and the flight surgeon.

- Privacy and consent: data stays on board, camera and microphone are opt-in, and crewmates only see a shared colour with consent.

- Usability under stress: one status, one action, large icons, and languages for the website (EN/ES/FR/DE).

- Scientific grounding: NASA-STD-3001, NASA HRP, NASA Twins Study, NEWS2 and over 70 referenced sources.

HONEST LIMITS: Open astronaut data is scarce, so the system is designed to learn from Earth recordings and recalibrate to each person; the demo runs on simulated data. The sensors (wearables, cabin sensors, camera and microphone) are specified, not built, and the camera and microphone are indirect indicators of stress and fatigue, not diagnostic tools. Thresholds and weights are illustrative and need clinical validation. The system has not been tested with users or crews, and the adaptive-normality concept is not yet validated with flight data. We went deep on one scenario, so other modules are presented at design level and left to the roadmap. COSMOS + VISION is decision support, not a medical device.
